topics: ☠️ New Mishna: Which Sin Offerings Are 'Left to Die'?
🔄 The Second, Recovered Animal — Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's contradictory-looking rulings
👥 'A Community Does Not Die' — Rav Pappa's proof from Temple treasury funds
📜 Ezra's Puzzling Sin Offerings — sacrificed generations after the sin, by intentional sinners
🐐 The Pious Man's Goat — a digression on the 'clusters' of unblemished Sages

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Sin Offerings Left to Die, and a Community That Cannot
overview.subtitle: Temurah 15a–15b
overview.hebrewSource: חַטַּאת הַיָּחִיד שֶׁכִּפְּרוּ בְּעָלֶיהָ — מֵתָה, וְשֶׁל צִבּוּר — אֵינָהּ מֵתָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna states a halakha from Sinai: five kinds of disqualified sin offerings must be left to die rather than redeemed, including one whose owner already achieved atonement with a replacement. This applies to an individual's sin offering but not the community's — a point Rabbi Yehuda disputes, and which Rabbi Shimon defends by analogy to other cases unique to individuals. The Gemara untangles a contradiction in how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon are each quoted on the animal recovered after a replacement was already brought. Rav Pappa then explains why a communal sin offering never 'dies' even when some contributors have died: a community itself cannot die. This leads to Ezra 8:35's puzzling sin offerings — sacrificed generations after the sin, by people whose idolatry was intentional — explained as a provisional wartime-like edict. The daf closes with a moving digression on the generations of unblemished Torah scholars and a story about a suspiciously misjudged goat.

slides.title: ☠️ New Mishna: Sin Offerings 'Left to Die'
slides.subtitle: A halakha from Sinai, with individual/communal at its center
rows: Owner achieved atonement via a replacement
Rabbi Shimon: not left to die (Rabbi Yehuda dissents: also left to die)

callout.label: Rabbi Shimon's method:
callout.text: He argues by pattern: since the first three cases plainly apply only to an individual's offering, the fourth and fifth (offering whose year passed) must follow the same pattern.

slides.title: 🔄 Whose Ruling Is It — Graze or Die?
slides.subtitle: A baraita seems to contradict what the mishna already told us

lines.speaker: Baraita (as first read)
lines.text: If one's lost sin offering is later found (after a replacement was already brought and sacrificed), Rabbi Yehuda says the extra animal should GRAZE until blemished; Rabbi Shimon says it should DIE.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But that's backwards! Our mishna already told us Rabbi Yehuda holds the animal DIES, and it's Rabbi Shimon's five-case list that includes this very scenario as one that dies!

lines.speaker: First resolution
lines.text: Don't swap the names — instead distinguish the CASES: the baraita discusses an animal found lost only at the time of SEPARATING the replacement (found before the replacement was sacrificed) — hence it may graze. The mishna discusses one still lost at the time of ATONEMENT itself.

lines.speaker: Alternative resolution
lines.text: Or: both sources discuss the same timing, but two versions of Rabbi Yehuda exist — one following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's stricter view (dies even if found before sacrifice), one following the Rabbis' more lenient view (graze, since found before sacrifice).

callout.label: Lesson:
callout.text: Apparent contradictions between parallel sources are often resolved by identifying a subtle difference in the case, not by assuming an error.

slides.title: 👥 Why Doesn't a Communal Sin Offering 'Die'?
slides.subtitle: Rav Pappa's principle: אֵין הַצִּיבּוּר מֵתִים — a community does not die

nodes.content: ❓ If SOME of the community's contributors die before the offering is sacrificed, shouldn't the same 'owner died' rule apply?
💬 Rav Pappa: No — a community, as an entity, never 'dies,' regardless of individual deaths
📜 Proof: Communal Festival/New Moon goat offerings are funded from the Temple treasury chamber (תְּרוּמַת הַלִּשְׁכָּה), collected once a year
✅ Some of THAT year's donors surely die before their offering is sacrificed months later — yet the offerings proceed without issue. The 'owner died' rule simply doesn't touch communal offerings

callout.label: Why not just 'sons replace fathers'?
callout.text: The Gemara rejects deriving this from Psalms 45:17 ('your sons instead of your fathers'), since that would extend the leniency even to individuals, which is not the halakha.

slides.title: 📜 Ezra's Sin Offerings, Generations Late
slides.subtitle: How could returning exiles bring sin offerings for a sin they hadn't unwittingly committed?
slides.label: The puzzle and its answer:
slides.text: Ezra 8:35 records twelve goat sin offerings brought by those returning from Babylonian exile — for the sin of idolatry committed generations earlier, in King Zedekiah's time. Two problems: sin offerings normally atone only for UNWITTING sin, yet idolatry under Zedekiah was intentional; and if the offering was for the dead generation, how could 'a community doesn't die' even apply, since these seem to be for people long gone? Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves the first difficulty: this was a הוֹרָאַת שָׁעָה, a provisional emergency ruling permitting sin offerings even for intentional sin. And the Gemara notes a supporting detail — the offering's odd count (12 bulls and goats for the 12 tribes, but 96 rams and 77 lambs corresponding to no obvious structure) itself signals this was an improvised, one-time exception rather than a standard sacrifice.

slides.title: 🐐 A Digression: The Last Unblemished 'Clusters'
slides.subtitle: From Yosef ben Yo'ezer's death to a story about wrongful suspicion

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'From the death of Yosef ben Yo'ezer and Yosef ben Yoḥanan, the אֶשְׁכּוֹלוֹת (clusters — scholars 'containing all') ceased' — and Torah was no longer studied exactly 'like Moses'
2️⃣ Challenge: doesn't a baraita say 3,000 halakhot were already forgotten in Moses' own mourning period? Answer: what wasn't forgotten stayed learned at that level
3️⃣ Story: a pious man used a goat's milk as medicine (tied to his bed); his friends suspected him of harboring 'an armed bandit' (a crop-destroying animal) — until they found this was his ONLY flaw
4️⃣ The man himself, dying, agreed: his sole sin was violating the Sages' ban on raising small livestock in inhabited Eretz Yisrael

callout.label: The point:
callout.text: Later generations (Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai) could still be flawless in this way — proving unblemished piety didn't end with the earliest 'clusters.'

summary.principle: Five kinds of disqualified sin offerings are left to die by a halakha from Sinai, but this applies only to an individual's offering — a community, which cannot 'die,' is never subject to this rule, even when its offering follows generations after the sin it atones for.

flowSteps.content: ☠️ Mishna: individual sin offering (atoned via replacement) dies; communal does not (R' Yehuda dissents)
🔄 Apparent Yehuda/Shimon contradiction resolved by distinguishing timing or by two versions of R' Yehuda

columns.content: 👥 Rav Pappa: a community never 'dies,' proven from treasury-funded goats
📜 Ezra's late sin offerings: a provisional emergency ruling

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: the halakha of a sin offering 'left to die' is inherently a rule about individuals, not the collective

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is the key difference between an individual's sin offering and a communal sin offering when the owner already achieved atonement via a replacement?
o: Both are left to die
The individual's offering is left to die; the communal offering is not (Rabbi Yehuda dissents)
Neither is ever left to die
Only the communal offering is left to die
quiz.e: The mishna rules that an individual's sin offering in this situation is left to die, while a communal sin offering is not — though Rabbi Yehuda holds even a communal offering should die.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve the apparent contradiction between the mishna (Rabbi Yehuda: dies) and a baraita (seemingly Rabbi Yehuda: graze) about the recovered sin offering?
o: It concludes one of the sources must be a forgery

It distinguishes the timing of when the original animal was found (before sacrifice of the replacement vs. still lost at the time of atonement), or attributes the difference to two versions of Rabbi Yehuda's view
It says Rabbi Yehuda never actually existed
It simply ignores the contradiction
quiz.e: The Gemara offers two resolutions: distinguishing whether the original animal was found before or after the replacement's sacrifice, or attributing the difference to Rabbi Yehuda's view aligning with either Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi or the Rabbis in a related dispute.

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa, why doesn't the 'owner died' rule apply to communal sin offerings, even though individual contributors inevitably die before the offering is sacrificed?
o: Because communal offerings are never actually sacrificed
Because a community itself does not 'die,' unlike an individual owner
Because the Temple treasury refunds all contributions
Because only priests contribute to communal offerings
quiz.e: Rav Pappa's principle, proven from the ongoing use of treasury-chamber funds for Festival and New Moon goat offerings despite the deaths of some contributors, is that a community as a collective entity cannot 'die.'

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan explain the sin offerings described in Ezra 8:35, brought generations after the sin of idolatry under King Zedekiah, given that idolatry was committed intentionally?
o: He says the verse is not really describing sin offerings
He explains it was a הוֹרָאַת שָׁעָה — a provisional emergency ruling permitting sin offerings even for an intentional sin
He says only unintentional idolaters were included
He denies the offerings were ever brought
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves the difficulty (sin offerings normally atone only for unwitting sin) by explaining this was a one-time provisional ruling (horaat sha'ah) suited to the exceptional circumstances of the return from exile.

quiz.q: In the story of the pious man and the goat, what turned out to be his only transgression?
o: Idol worship
Keeping a goat in his house in violation of the Sages' ban on raising small livestock in inhabited Eretz Yisrael
Failing to pray
Theft
quiz.e: Despite his friends' initial alarm at seeing the goat (fearing it signaled something sinister), a thorough examination — confirmed by the man himself on his deathbed — found his only sin was keeping the goat, violating the rabbinic prohibition against raising small livestock in settled areas of Eretz Yisrael.
